articles.title: Prédio do antigo hotel Maksoud Plaza, primeiro cinco estrelas de SP, tem projeto de condomínio com 550 unidades | G1
articles.standfirst: Pedido de alvará de reforma está em análise na prefeitura. Projeto também prevê cinco lojas e cerca de 595 vagas de estacionamento. Inaugurado em 1979 e fechado em 2021, hotel recebeu celebridades internacionais, entre elas Frank Sinatra e Michael Jackson.
articles.summary: Pedido de alvará de reforma está em análise na prefeitura. Projeto também prevê cinco lojas e cerca de 595 vagas de estacionamento. Inaugurado em 1979 e fechado em 2021, hotel recebeu celebridades internacionais, entre elas Frank Sinatra e Michael Jackson.
articles.body:
Hotel Maksoud — Foto: Instagram Hotel Maksoud/reprodução

O prédio de 23 andares que abrigou o tradicional hotel Maksoud Plaza, na Bela Vista, em São Paulo , está vazio desde dezembro de 2021, quando o estabelecimento encerrou definitivamente as atividades após 42 anos. Quatro anos depois, um projeto de reforma apresentado à Prefeitura prevê transformar o imóvel em um empreendimento de uso misto, com 398 unidades residenciais e outras 152 destinadas a serviços de hospedagem.

O pedido de Alvará de Aprovação de Reforma está em análise na Prefeitura de São Paulo. Segundo a Secretaria Municipal de Urbanismo e Licenciamento (SMUL), o projeto prevê um conjunto com seis subsolos, térreo e 26 pavimentos.

Além das 398 unidades residenciais e das 152 destinadas a serviços de hospedagem, também estão previstas cinco lojas com fachada ativa. O empreendimento contempla aproximadamente 595 vagas de estacionamento, distribuídas entre os usos residenciais e não residenciais.

A Prefeitura não informou a data em que o pedido foi protocolado e afirmou que não há prazo previsto para a conclusão da análise. O processo segue em tramitação, com a verificação do cumprimento da legislação urbanística e edilícia vigente.

O projeto é assinado pelo escritório Metro Arquitetos Associados, informação antecipada pela revista Exame e confirmada pelo g1 .

Procurado, o escritório, que tem no portfólio o novo prédio do Masp, informou a participação, mas disse que não está autorizado a fornecer detalhes técnicos, conceituais ou de execução devido ao contrato de confidencialidade com o cliente.

Inaugurado em 1979, o Maksoud Plaza foi o primeiro hotel cinco estrelas de São Paulo e se tornou um dos endereços mais conhecidos da hotelaria de luxo na cidade.

O edifício foi um dos primeiros do país a contar com um amplo saguão central com pé-direito alto, que integra visualmente os diferentes andares, além de elevadores panorâmicos. Ao longo de seus 42 anos de funcionamento, recebeu personalidades da música, do cinema e da política internacional.

Entre os hóspedes estiveram os cantores Michael Jackson, Axl Rose, Ray Charles e os integrantes dos Rolling Stones ; os atores e diretores Quentin Tarantino, Catherine Deneuve e Pedro Almodóvar; os príncipes Rainier e Albert, de Mônaco; e a então primeira-ministra britânica Margaret Thatcher.

O cantor norte-americano Michael Jackson é visto durante apresentação no Estádio do Morumbi, em São Paulo, em São Paulo, outubro de 1993. O cantor ficou hospedado no Maksoud Plaza durante sua estadia em São Paulo — Foto: Célio Jr/Estadão Conteúdo/Arquivo

Uma das apresentações mais marcantes aconteceu em 1981, quando Frank Sinatra se apresentou no Salão Nobre do hotel. Anos depois, em 2015, o cantor foi homenageado com a inauguração do Frank Bar, que entrou para a lista dos melhores bares do mundo da publicação World's 50 Best Bars.

Outro espaço que marcou a história do Maksoud foi o 150 Night Club, uma das casas de espetáculos mais disputadas do Brasil nas décadas de 1980 e 1990. O local recebeu apresentações de artistas como Tom Jobim, Julio Iglesias, Bobby Short, Alberta Hunter, Etta James, Billy Eckstine, Buddy Guy e Dorival Caymmi.

Frank Sinatra em seu show no Maksoud Plaza, em São Paulo, em agosto de 1981 — Foto: Acervo Maksoud Plaza via BBC

O hotel também ficou conhecido por episódios envolvendo seus hóspedes. Em dezembro de 1992, Axl Rose, vocalista do Guns N' Roses, se irritou com a presença de jornalistas no local e atirou uma cadeira do mezanino em direção aos repórteres que estavam no térreo.

Michael Jackson se hospedou no Maksoud em 1993 , quando esteve em São Paulo para um show no Estádio do Morumbi.

Em novembro de 1995, a cantora Sheryl Crow concedeu uma entrevista coletiva no hotel. Quentin Tarantino também aproveitou as dependências do estabelecimento para atender a imprensa durante uma passagem pela cidade, em outubro de 2006.

Já entre os brasileiros que passaram pelo local estão João Gilberto, Gonzaguinha e Martinho da Vila.

Hotel teve o primeiro elevador panorâmico da cidade — Foto: Divulgação/ Maksoud Plaza

O Maksoud Plaza fechou definitivamente as portas em 7 de dezembro de 2021 , depois de 42 anos de atividades. Na época, o hotel operava com apenas 20% da capacidade e não resistiu aos prejuízos financeiros.

Segundo a HM Hotéis, administradora do Maksoud, e a Hidroservice Engenharia, controladora do hotel, os últimos hóspedes deixaram o estabelecimento ao meio-dia do dia anterior ao encerramento das atividades. Os clientes que tinham reservas futuras seriam reembolsados.

Na ocasião, a HM Hotéis informou que pretendia continuar no segmento de hospitalidade e manter a marca Maksoud Plaza. A empresa buscava parceiros para um projeto com a marca em um novo endereço.

O processo de desmontagem do espaço começou no próprio dia do fechamento. A empresa tinha até 31 de dezembro daquele ano para entregar o prédio.

Início da obra do hotel — Foto: Divulgação/ Maksoud Plaza

O fechamento ocorreu em meio a uma crise financeira e a uma disputa envolvendo o patrimônio do Grupo Maksoud.

Em 2020, a HM Hotéis e a Hidroservice Engenharia entraram com um pedido de recuperação judicial de R$ 81 milhões, sem considerar as dívidas tributárias, na Justiça de São Paulo.

Com o processo, as empresas conseguiram reduzir pela metade as dívidas incluídas na recuperação judicial e alongar os prazos de pagamento para até 23 anos. A exceção eram os créditos trabalhistas, que deveriam ser quitados em até 12 meses.

O grupo também renegociou débitos que não estavam incluídos no processo, como as dívidas tributárias. O endividamento fiscal federal foi reduzido em mais de 60%, e o saldo restante foi parcelado em até dez anos.

A disputa pelo prédio também se arrastou na Justiça. O imóvel e o terreno onde funcionava o hotel foram arrematados em 2011 pelos irmãos Fernando e Jussara Simões, empresários do grupo JSL, em um leilão da Justiça do Trabalho destinado ao pagamento de dívidas trabalhistas de empresas do Grupo Maksoud.

O leilão, porém, foi suspenso judicialmente, e as partes entraram em acordo para encerrar a disputa. A HM Hotéis deveria entregar o edifício, mas os irmãos Simões só tomaram posse do local em 2022.

Em 2021, o Tribunal de Justiça de São Paulo determinou que o hotel fosse lacrado e que os móveis fossem recolhidos. A decisão foi tomada após um pedido dos filhos do fundador Henry Maksoud, que questionavam a forma como o acordo havia sido firmado e os prazos estabelecidos.

O desembargador Araldo Telles, da 2ª Câmara Reservada de Direito Empresarial, determinou a suspensão da imissão na posse dos arrematantes até 30 de janeiro de 2022, além da lacração do imóvel e da arrecadação dos bens móveis que estavam no local.

Leilão dos itens do Maksoud Plaza: lote com 143 poltronas floridas, como a da foto, foi arrematado por R$ 95 mil. — Foto: Reprodução/FCR Leilões

Depois do fechamento, os objetos que faziam parte da estrutura do Maksoud Plaza também foram colocados à venda.

Em agosto de 2022, um leilão de bens do hotel já havia arrecadado mais de R$ 1,3 milhão. Entre os itens vendidos estavam cadeiras, colchões, máquinas de costura e equipamentos utilizados na operação do estabelecimento.

Um dos lotes mais curiosos reuniu 143 poltronas floridas, arrematadas por R$ 95.476,40, o equivalente a uma média de aproximadamente R$ 670 por unidade.

Também foram vendidas 1,1 mil cadeiras utilizadas em eventos, 505 colchões, cinco máquinas de costura e uma máquina de sorvete, arrematada por R$ 4.480.

articles.title: Deirdre Keane: The ‘stubborn and determined’ New York runner has already completed 74 marathons; this year, she ran 7 of them while pregnant, finishing NYC Race at 34 weeks
articles.summary: Most people treat running one marathon, the 42.2-kilometre race, as a badge of honor.
articles.body: Most people treat running one marathon, the 42.2-kilometre race, as a badge of honor. After months of preparation, painful training, physical endurance, mental grit, and sheer willpower, it’s a feat that feels almost superhuman.But Deirdre Keane — she blew past that mark ages ago.In 2026, the 38-year-old New Yorker hit another level, running seven marathons while pregnant. She even finished the legendary New York City Marathon at 34 weeks, barely a month before her due date. And it wasn’t just another race; she managed to complete all seven World Marathon Majors in a single calendar year, which sounds like a goal that leaves most runners dreaming, never doing.Deirdre Keane: The runner who just won’t quitPer AP News, at 38, Deirdre Keane has already logged 74 marathons and ultramarathons. Her day job? She’s a nurse practitioner and health management consultant. But her recent accomplishment wasn’t just about tallying races; it’s the wild circumstances that grabbed everyone’s attention. Running all those miles while pregnant? She calls herself “stubborn and determined,” and honestly, it might be an understatement.But her marathon journey isn’t just about sporting ambition. It’s woven through a story of loss, personal courage, careful decisions, and a lifelong love for running.How Deirdre Keane pulled off seven marathons while pregnantKeane mapped out her 2026 marathon spree as a ‘do-it-before-kids’ project. She and her husband Brian had just gotten married in 2025, and figured pregnancy could take a while. So she signed up for a wild schedule: 11 events, seven World Marathon Majors, an Ironman, two ultras, a trail marathon in Ireland. Tokyo kicked things off in March. As Boston and London rolled around in April, she started feeling ‘off’: slower, out of sync. A pregnancy test settled it.The news could’ve derailed her plans. Instead, she reworked her marathon calendar. Her husband worried, not surprisingly, as he wondered if pounding out 26 miles while pregnant was even safe. After digging around for research, they realized there wasn’t a clear roadmap. Together, they decided to take each race step by step. She kept her pace slow, walking when needed, listening to her body more than ever.She checked in with her OB-GYN, who gave her the green light as long as she stayed hydrated, watched for warning signs like muscle cramps, and bailed if anything felt wrong.From there, she just kept going. According to her account to The Associated Press, Keane completed the Sydney Marathon in August at 25 weeks pregnant, Berlin in September at 29 weeks, and Chicago at 31 weeks. Then she did the New York Race at a whopping 34 weeks. The New York City Marathon took her just over four hours, which is a far cry from her sub-three-hour time the year before, but every bit as impressive.Keane finished the New York City Marathon in 4 hours, 6 minutes and 55 seconds, averaging approximately 9 minutes and 26 seconds per mile. For perspective, she had completed the same race in just over three hours in 2025. "I knew how bizarre it was to be running a marathon at 34 weeks, but I also knew how fit I was and self-aware of my body at this point," she told the AP.Of course, running so late in pregnancy made her nervous. She felt her body changing, knew she couldn’t push like before. Brian supported her on the course, handing her water, cheering her on. Friends leapt in too. The route even passed the hospital where she planned to deliver. She joked about stopping right there and having the baby.From running in her father's memory to completing 74 marathonsInterestingly, Keane’s deep relationship with running began young. Her dad, John, moved to the US from Ireland. He was a marathon runner himself in the 80s and 90s, even while battling cancer. He ran the New York City Marathon one day before major surgery, which speaks to the astonishing determination that runs in their genes. Keane lost him at 13, but his resilience shaped her.In college, she ran her first marathon as a tribute. Instead of just honoring her dad, she found a new passion. “I loved marathons from the beginning,” she explained. “They show what the human body can do, not just physically, but mentally.”Running mattered even more during the pandemic. Working as a nurse practitioner at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, the stress was relentless. Running became her lifeline: her escape from isolation, from emotional burnout.Keane eventually stretched her limits further by entering the World Marathon Challenge in 2023: seven marathons, seven continents, seven days. She took home the “fastest woman” title that year.Her World Marathon Majors project was the latest milestone. These races, including Tokyo, Boston, London, Sydney, Berlin, Chicago, and New York, draw the world’s best, each one notorious for its own challenges.Is it safe to run marathons while pregnant?Keane’s story kicked off heated debates about pregnancy, women’s endurance, and what’s possible for mothers-to-be. Many admire her achievement. Plenty question it. Is it worth the risk? Is it safe?Doctors urge people not to treat her journey as advice for everyone. There’s nuance. In a Washington Post report, exercise scientist Margie Davenport said that research now supports the idea that women who were fit pre-pregnancy can keep up intensive training, but with precautions. The key is to listen to the body, adjust when needed, and always have medical guidance.After all, pregnancy isn’t a one-size-fits-all restriction. Some women might keep running; others need to dial back. Even seasoned athletes sometimes need to stop and rethink.What’s next for Deirdre Keane?Keane made her decision after consulting doctors, adjusting her training, and always putting health first. Now, as her marathon journey winds down, she’s switching gears, prepping for motherhood.She hopes her grit spills over into her son’s life. “I want to teach my son resilience, that he can do hard things,” she says. When life gets rough, he’ll know persistence beats quitting. For someone who’s conquered 74 marathon finish lines, this lesson might just be the most significant yet.You use AI every day. articles.summary: A birthday sleepover in Oregon has become the centre of an $8.7 million negligence lawsuit after a 14-year-old boy suffered life-changing injuries in an
articles.body: A birthday sleepover in Oregon has become the centre of an $8.7 million negligence lawsuit after a 14-year-old boy suffered life-changing injuries in an electric bicycle crash. His mother, Alexis Nicoli, has filed a case against the parents who allegedly provided the children with e-bikes during the gathering. The incident, which took place in November 2025, was reported by KOIN 6 News and The Oregonian, with further details published by the Lake Oswego Review. According to the lawsuit, Nicoli’s son was attending a birthday sleepover at the home of Tessa and Matthew Cohen in the Portland area, along with another friend. The gathering was being held for the Cohens’ son, and the couple allegedly made several electric bicycles available to the boys to ride.The accident occurred while the children were riding together. Nicoli’s son reportedly lost control of the e-bike and crashed, sustaining severe injuries to his head and right eye. He was wearing a helmet at the time, according to the complaint. The teenager was rushed to hospital, where doctors identified multiple injuries, including a fracture to the inner wall of his right eye socket. The impact also caused a rupture that resulted in cerebrospinal fluid leaking from the area surrounding his brain and spinal cord.His injuries were so extensive that his right eye could not be saved. Doctors eventually replaced it with an orbital silicone sphere. The lawsuit also describes the extensive medical treatment required to address the damage to his skull and the surrounding structures. Nicoli is seeking $8.7 million in damages, arguing that the injuries have caused significant physical and psychological trauma and will affect her son’s life for years to come.Why the parents are being suedThe lawsuit accuses the Cohens of negligence, alleging that they allowed children who were not legally old enough to ride the electric bicycles to use them without adequate supervision. It also claims that the couple failed to establish whether the bikes were suitable and safe for the boys, provide proper instructions for their use or take reasonable precautions to prevent an accident. The case places particular emphasis on the responsibility of adults hosting children at their homes, especially when potentially dangerous recreational equipment is made available to young guests. The Cohens had not publicly responded to the allegations when KOIN 6 News published its report. The claims in the lawsuit have not been established in court.What Oregon’s e-bike rules sayOregon has specific age restrictions for electric bicycle riders, with the rules depending on the classification of the vehicle. Under the regulations applicable at the time of the November 2025 accident, riders generally had to be at least 16 to operate Class 2 and Class 3 e-bikes. Class 1 bicycles, which provide motor assistance only while pedalling and stop assisting at 20 mph, had a separate exemption for younger riders under the state’s earlier legislation.Further changes under House Bill 4007 will allow riders aged 14 and 15 to operate Class 1 e-bikes from January 1, 2027, while the minimum age for Class 2 and Class 3 models remains 16. The distinction could be significant in the lawsuit, as the precise classification of the bicycles provided to the children will be relevant to the allegations surrounding their use.As the case moves forward, the lawsuit is likely to draw attention to the responsibilities of parents who provide electric bicycles to children, particularly when hosting gatherings where several young riders may be involved.You use AI every day. articles.title: A pensioner in his 80s lost €10,000 after scammers posing as undercover police officers told him to withdraw cash for a secret investigation; a collector picked it up from his home
articles.summary: A routine phone call can sometimes be enough to set a fraud in motion, particularly when the person on the other end claims to represent an authority.
articles.body: A routine phone call can sometimes be enough to set a fraud in motion, particularly when the person on the other end claims to represent an authority. In Lancashire, a pensioner in his 80s was persuaded to withdraw €10,000 from his savings after callers posing as undercover police officers told him his bank account had been compromised. The money was collected from his home by a man whose identity remains unknown. What followed raised further concerns for investigating officers: the alleged fraudsters continued calling the victim's landline even while police were at his property looking into the incident. Lancashire Police are now working to trace those involved.How the pensioner was persuaded to withdraw the moneyThe incident involved a man living in Nelson, Lancashire. According to Lancashire Police, he received a telephone call from someone presenting themselves as an undercover police officer. The caller claimed there was a problem with his bank account and suggested that he needed to help with an investigation into suspected financial wrongdoing.The instructions involved withdrawing cash rather than transferring money electronically. The pensioner was told to obtain two separate sums of €5,000, taking the total to €10,000. He visited a local Post Office twice, on 21 and 22 January 2026, to withdraw the money.The use of euros was part of the arrangement. The amount involved was equivalent to approximately £8,706 at the time reported by the BBC. After the withdrawals, an unidentified man arrived at the pensioner's home and collected the cash. It was only later that the victim became suspicious about what had happened. He contacted Lancashire Police to report his concerns that he had been deceived.Callers continued contacting his home during the police investigationThe investigation took an unusual turn when officers discovered that the callers had not stopped trying to reach the pensioner. While police were at his property examining the circumstances of the suspected fraud, further calls came through to his landline. The calls were made from a withheld telephone number. Police said members of the organised crime group continued attempting to contact the victim even as officers were present at the address.The incident has prompted detectives to work towards identifying those responsible and locating the person who collected the money. The force confirmed that the pensioner was receiving support and safeguarding assistance following the incident. There has been no public confirmation of arrests in the case in the BBC report dated 26 January 2026.Police warn against requests to withdraw money for investigationsLancashire Police used the incident to remind residents that legitimate officers and bank employees do not ask members of the public to withdraw cash as part of secret or undercover fraud investigations. A caller claiming to be a police officer may sound convincing, particularly if they speak about supposed criminal activity involving a person's finances. However, a request to take money out of a bank account and hand it to an unknown individual should be treated as a serious warning sign.The force advised anyone who is uncertain about the identity of a caller claiming to be a police officer to ask for their name and identification details. Those details should then be checked independently by contacting the genuine police.Its advice was to call 999 if there are concerns about someone claiming to be an officer. People should not rely on a telephone number supplied by the caller or assume that an incoming call is genuine simply because the person appears to know personal or financial details. For the pensioner in Nelson, the two withdrawals resulted in a loss of €10,000. Detectives continue to pursue enquiries into the suspected organised fraud, while the victim is being supported by police.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available reports and information released by Lancashire Police. articles.title: Staff gagging clauses lifted ahead of probe into culture at data watchdog
articles.summary: Ministers are expected to publish the details of how an independent review of the working environment at the Information Commission will be carried out next week.
articles.body:
Non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) signed by staff at the UK's information watchdog will be lifted to allow them to speak out about its culture, the government has confirmed.

Ministers are expected to publish the details of how an independent review of the working environment at the Information Commission will be carried out next week.

It follows the departure of the watchdog's boss five months ago amid allegations of sexually inappropriate behaviour.

A government spokesperson confirmed that NDAs, known as "gagging clauses", would not be enforced by the Information Commission, saying the regulator "will not use the terms of any agreement to prevent people from participating in the review".

The government "will set out further details on the review, including its terms of reference and the independent reviewer, shortly", they added.

The Information Commission is one of the UK's most high-profile regulators charged with the crucial task of regulating AI, data protection and Freedom of Information requests.

It recently won a court battle with TikTok after it fined the social media platform £12.7m for misusing children's data, and has penalised bodies including the Ministry of Defence after an email blunder exposed the details of interpreters fleeing Afghanistan.

But it has been without permanent leadership since Information Commissioner John Edwards resigned earlier this year .

It came after an independent investigation found a "case to answer" over reports of alleged inappropriate behaviour towards staff including claims of sexual harassment.

The Information Commission said the investigation found Edwards' behaviour "fell short of the conduct expected from a public official".

In a resignation statement posted on his LinkedIn page in June, Edwards said he disagreed with how the investigation had been carried out but accepted his position had "become untenable".

The statement continued: "I have accepted that there have been occasions where I exercised poor judgement and made attempts at humour that were inappropriate and caused offence."

Freedom of Information requests have found that since the start of Edwards' tenure in 2022 to the present, 16 current and former employees have signed non-disclosure or confidentiality clauses costing more than £354,000.

Nine of those included a "non-derogatory clause" which legally prevents employees from making negative comments publicly.

While this is a small proportion of the more than 1,000 staff employed by the commissioner, government advice stipulates that public bodies should only use confidentiality clauses "when necessary" and that they should "not seek to stifle or discourage staff from raising concerns".

Since 2025, new laws also mean they cannot be used to silence employees subjected to harassment or abuse.

After Edwards' departure, the government announced a review into the Commission's culture and governance, with the then-Secretary of State for Science, Innovation and Technology Liz Kendall telling a committee of MPs she was "absolutely appalled at what the independent investigator found - sexual harassment and bullying".

Five months later, the investigation has not begun.

In recent weeks, the two major civil service unions, the PCS and FDA, have pushed for an external examination of the events leading up to Edwards' resignation in meetings with government officials.

The unions have also asked for those who signed non-disclosure agreements with the ICO to be released from them so they can contribute to the review.

The PCS union says other concerns had previously been raised with them about Edwards, including a bullying complaint, which was investigated at the time.

An internal staff survey, published in August and released under FOI points towards wider issues at the Commission, with 14% of all employees reporting they had either personally experienced bullying, harassment and discrimination.

Multiple current and former employees have also told the BBC of experiencing or witnessing incidents of bullying or harassment.

PCS General Secretary Fran Heathcote said the union's members at the Commission "have been failed for too long by a toxic leadership culture that has allowed bullying and harassment to persist, leaving many staff fearful of speaking out".

Heathcote said she welcomed the "positive engagement" the union had received in recent weeks from the Commission and officials at the Department for Culture Media and Sport (DCMS), which oversees it.

But she added: "For the review to command the confidence of staff, it must be genuinely independent, robust in its approach, and prepared to identify where accountability lies."

Conservative MP Caroline Dinenage, who chairs the DCMS select committee, said the Commission "needed a firm new direction" after the departure of its former boss.

"Instead, a leadership vacuum has compounded what went before at a rudderless organisation where it seems the worst behaviours in the workplace are not being challenged," she added.

She said it was "vital" the government brought in "someone who can set a new tone and is dedicated to changing attitudes and protecting staff" to head up the Commission.

A spokesperson for the Information Commission said its commitment to an independent review reflected its "ongoing commitment to listening and learning from the events of the past year and those leading up to it".

"Our new Board, appointed this summer, has been working exceptionally hard to provide fresh leadership, ushering in a new governance structure and a new strategy," they added.

"It is committed to listening carefully to the review's findings and recommendations, and building on the positive work on our culture already taking place across the organisation."

articles.title: The Darkness to headline Norwich festival as homecoming gig
articles.summary: Frontman Justin Hawkins says he plans to be "as loud as possible" headlining the Rock N Roll Circus.
articles.body:
The frontman of The Darkness says he plans to be "as loud as possible" as the band prepares to play a homecoming gig.

The band will headline the final night of the Rock N Roll Circus festival on 22 August 2027 at Earlham Park in Norwich.

Justin Hawkins, from Lowestoft, said that while it was rare to play an outdoor event in East Anglia, he saw his first ever live concert in Norwich when the hard rock band Thunder played the University of East Anglia in 1991.

He said: "We're coming home! Well, very nearly. Norwich is close enough to Lowestoft for us to consider this a homecoming, and what better way to do it than under a giant circus tent with an absolutely outrageous collection of rock bands?"

Speaking to Chris Goreham on BBC Radio Norfolk, Hawkins recalled his formative years of music in and around East Anglia.

"That first show, Luke Morley was the guitar player in Thunder... he's the reason why I started playing a white [Gibson] Les Paul - as he was playing one when I saw him," he said.

"It changes everything — the formative exposure to live music is really important."

"There used to be a really good coastal circuit," he added. "Bands like Dire Straits and the Rolling Stones used to play places like Great Yarmouth, Lowestoft and various other seaside resorts and that probably stopped due to logistics and licensing regulations.

"For some reason it stopped and that's a real shame and I want to try and bring that back."

The Rock N Roll Circus festival will return to Norwich for its third year with headline acts also featuring the Blossoms and the Kaiser Chiefs.

It aims to bring together some of the biggest names in British rock and indie music, alongside circus entertainment.

Hawkins said: "We are going to try and be as loud as possible.

"When I look at that line-up I think what an honour to play among those other artists - especially The Cult - I can't quite believe we are going on after them. It's going to be a difficult one to follow, one of my favourite bands of all time. Obviously [it's] a massive honour. I can't wait to do it.

"Putting on a festival is very challenging... for it to be successful is a great achievement. We are very happy to be part of the next phase of it."

articles.title: UK weather: Lowest overnight temperatures of autumn as cold alerts in force
articles.summary: Temperatures dropped well below freezing in many areas on Friday night but how long will the chilly weather last?
articles.body:
Much of the UK has experienced a widespread frost overnight - with temperatures dropping as low as -10.6C in some areas.

Northern areas have borne the brunt of the chill with the lowest temperature recorded at Tulloch Bridge.

Following the cold and frosty start, dry and sunny weather will dominate across many parts of the UK over the weekend, once any patchy fog clears - although rain will arrive in some southern and western areas on Sunday.

Cold health alerts , external issued by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) for northern England have been extended until Tuesday morning.

Northern and central areas of the UK will stay chilly over the weekend with highs in some parts of Scotland and northern England reaching only 4C on Saturday.

More widely, afternoon temperatures in most of central and eastern England, as well as Northern Ireland, will tend to hover around 7-10C.

The yellow cold health alerts issued by the UKHSA, in conjunction with the Met Office, cover north-west and north-east England as well as Yorkshire and the Humber. They have been extended and are now in place until 09:00 GMT on Tuesday.

They warn of the risk of minor impacts on health and social care services, with greater use of healthcare services by vulnerable people - who will face an increased risk to life.

While most places will enjoy a largely sunny weekend thanks to the clear Arctic air, which has spread across the UK from the north, a weather front will begin to nudge into parts of south-west England and Wales bringing something of a change.

It means cloud and outbreaks of persistent rain will affect the far south-west of Wales, along with southern and western parts of England, on Sunday.

This will also usher in some milder air with temperatures likely to climb to 12-14C in the far south-west, in stark contrast to the rest of the country.

The UK will find itself in something of a battleground between high pressure, generally centred to the north and the east, and then rain and strengthening winds from the Atlantic.

This means the greatest chance of rain will - initially - be in western and southern areas with drier and sunnier conditions expected further north and east.

Later in the week there are signs from computer weather models that outbreaks of rain will make more progress eastwards.

Northerly winds will be replaced by a more easterly airflow. Temperatures are likely to be just below the seasonal average in most locations.

If the air is cold enough when weather fronts arrive it is possible that some rain could turn to snow over high ground, especially in the north of the UK, but there is a lot of uncertainty about that part of the forecast.

articles.title: How Westside Cowboy went from student gigs to rising stars in two years
articles.summary: The four-piece band joins a prestigious list that includes Myles Smith, Olivia Dean, Tom Grennan.
articles.body:
In two years, Westside Cowboy have rocketed from the sweaty corners of Manchester's student pub circuit to performances on one of America's biggest talk shows and at many of the UK's biggest festivals.

What started as jamming for fun in a student bedroom has become the latest revolution in British indie known as "Britainicana".

Now the quartet have been named the BBC Introducing Artist of the Year for 2026.

Westside Cowboy join a prestigious list that includes Myles Smith, Olivia Dean, Tom Grennan and several other now household names that have won the award.

But how did they get there, and so quickly?

It is 3 December 2024 and I am finally about to see Westside Cowboy.

A typical cold winter night on Oldham Street, Manchester, where four students are set to play their first headline show together in the innocuous backroom of a little pub called The Castle Hotel.

It was the launch night of their debut single I've Never Met Anyone I Thought I Could Really Love (Until I Met You).

It is a sub-three-minute explosion of some of the finest pop rock you could ever hope to hear.

They had released the single on 7 November 2024 and uploaded it to the BBC Introducing website on the same day.

I played it on BBC Introducing on BBC Radio Lancashire that very night, and quickly forwarded it to the BBC Introducing Mixtape.

It was soon played by Emily Pilbeam on BBC Radio 6Music.

Westside Cowboy had the attention of the nation's music media.

By the time their second single Shells was released in April 2025, Westside Cowboy had been selected by BBC Introducing to play on their illustrious stage at Glastonbury festival.

The song also went straight on to the coveted 6Music playlist.

Every other single the band have released since has received the same treatment and more.

Paddy Murphy, Reuben Haycocks and Aoife Anson O'Connell met in autumn 2021 at the Royal Northern College of Music on Oxford Road.

One day, Murphy and Haycocks walked down Oxford Road to Johnny Roadhouse, a music shop fronted with an array of hanging brass instruments and full of Manchester folklore.

It has served the city's musicians since 1955.

They ran into guitar repairer, Jimmy Bradbury, who asked Murphy and Haycocks if they fancied starting a band called Westside Cowboy.

Be grateful that the answer was yes - with O'Connell joining later that evening.

Murphy and Bradbury had been in a band together before, a surf-rock trio called Katz, and Murphy and Haycocks both played in another trio, DieKaiDie.

Drummer Murphy played guitar for another band too, Holly Head, however O'Connell had not even played a guitar before she picked up the bass for Westside Cowboy. She was a cellist.

It is safe to say that this new band had plenty of competition for their time, but nevertheless it was soon to be their top priority.

It all began in Paddy's student bedroom.

Sessions where the modus operandi was shaking off the pretensions of their other perhaps more lofty-minded projects, and taking things back to basics to rediscover the answer to the question of why they actually loved playing music - because it was fun.

Within a few short months they were one of the country's hottest underground prospects, with videos of their live shows spreading all over Instagram.

On 1 February 2025 I introduced them on stage.

Westside Cowboy were one of four local artists showcased by BBC Introducing at The Grand in Clitheroe.

It was a set laden with songs they would release in the subsequent 18 months.

Then in April, I was calling them from our radio studio to tell them that they had been awarded one of the coveted spots on the BBC Introducing stage at Glastonbury Festival 2025.

Westside Cowboy then also won Glastonbury's prestigious Emerging Talent Competition to perform on the Woodsies Stage alongside Blossoms and Scissor Sisters.

Loyal listeners to BBC Introducing in Lancashire & Cumbria followed every step of the band's progress through 2025.

Their claim to the show came courtesy of drummer Murphy, who grew up in the market town of Longridge, Lancashire, which sits a few miles north of Preston.

Imitations of his "Westsiiide Cowboooy!" scream became a regular feature, recognised as the only way to introduce the band's music on the radio.

The high point of 2025 for the band was the release of their first EP, which was recorded by Lewis Whiting, the guitarist from English Teacher.

Its title This Better Be Something Great wryly proclaimed the general astonishment at just how fast this little student band was blowing up.

The EP was used for the students' coursework at RNCM, and secured the band a contract with Island Records – the same label as Ariana Grande, Sabrina Carpenter, Florence + The Machine and English Teacher.

They were soon jetting off to New York to record their next EP with Loren Humphrey, whose reputation was soaring after the success of Heavy Metal - the debut solo album from Cameron Winter, the lead singer of Geese.

Westside Cowboy then headed to Paris for a 15-date European tour supporting their heroes, Black Country, New Road.

Their second EP was released in January 2026 titled So Much Country 'Till We Get There.

In the months that followed, Westside Cowboy were back touring Europe, this time opening for Geese, who had a decent claim for being the most exciting indie band in the world.

This was possibly the hottest support slot on the planet, and these four Manchester students had it.

They soon announced their own debut album It Goes On, which charted at No. 5 in the Official Album Charts.

After a performance on Later… with Jools Holland on BBC Two, Westside Cowboy were off to America again to make their US television debut on The Tonight Show starring Jimmy Fallon, one of the most recognisable TV shows in the world.

It was still under two years since their first headline show.

In a world where artists fiddle frustratingly at algorithms trying to get their music to an audience on platforms like TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, and Spotify, this is an old school meteoric rise the likes of which the music industry must have thought no longer possible.

It has been achieved by four seemingly ordinary students regularly seen wandering down Oxford Road in Manchester.

Together the have been named the outstanding emerging act of the year by the BBC Introducing.

articles.title: How online predator duped 70 girls into believing he loved them
articles.summary: Bilal Kazi led his victims to believe they were in a relationship with a 14-year-old boy named Reece.
articles.body:
Over the course of four years, student Bilal Kazi manipulated and groomed at least 70 girls from across the UK - but police fear there could be more than 100 further victims yet to be identified.

Kazi, who was aged between 22 and 26 at the time, led his victims to believe they were in a relationship with a 14-year-old boy named Reece.

The lead detective in the case, Det Con Georgia Hughes, said his crimes came to light only after one of the victims was "brave enough to go and report what had happened".

Kazi, who was a student from India studying at the University of Chester, would meet his victims online - most notably on Snapchat, Wink, and Roblox - always using the same method.

He provided a false photograph of a boy - who has not been identified - to aid his deception between August 2021 and August 2025.

"He would add the victim and he would very quickly start grooming them to believe that they were in a relationship," said Hughes.

"He would set out his expectations of that relationship very early on.

"So things such as never to be left on read, I want you to be clingy, I want you to be loyal to me."

Soon after, Kazi would ask the girls to send naked images of themselves, telling them that this is what you do when you love someone.

This would quickly progress to him asking the victims to send more explicit images and videos of themselves performing sexual acts.

"When they would question that, he would say 'well this is what you do when you love somebody and when you're in a relationship with somebody'," said Hughes, of Cheshire Police.

"For a lot of the victims this was their first ever relationship, their first ever experience of anything like this so they went along with it."

If the victims refused to send more images, he would then threaten to "leak" the images that had already been sent to him or recorded by himself covertly on Snapchat to their friends and family.

In some cases, Kazi hacked into victims' social media accounts, shared the content with their friends and published the pictures on social media.

Martin McRobb, a specialist prosecutor at the Crown Prosecution Service, said Kazi "acted with absolute ruthlessness in grooming, manipulating and exploiting a large number of young vulnerable girls".

"He befriended them online and forced them to take photos and videos carrying out sexual acts," he said.

"He then blackmailed those who refused to comply with his further demands, threatening to post the explicit imagery to others."

Kazi was circulated as wanted after the first victim came forward - but police were unable to trace him at first.

He was later arrested at Heathrow Airport as he re-entered the country on 21 July 2023.

His mobile phone was seized and 180 possible victims were identified.

Seventy of these victims were located from their usernames stored on Kazi's phone.

"It's fair to say that every victim that we visited was shocked about this," said Hughes.

"They really believed that they were speaking to Reece.

"A lot of them really believed that they'd been in a relationship with Reece and they thought that they loved this boy and that this boy loved them back.

"So they were very distressed finding out that who they were speaking to was absolutely not who he was portraying to be."

Kazi was released on bail following his arrest to a property in Birmingham with conditions, including not to leave the country.

A sexual risk order was imposed to manage him while investigations continued.

But he was later remanded in prison after he continued to contact girls online.

"There hasn't been any remorse," said Hughes.

"He was messaging girls all the time, every minute of every day, into late at night.

"It was multiple girls at the same time and just continuous offending that was quite incessant really.

"And it continued while he was on bail. He continued offending throughout the entire process until he was remanded in prison."

Kazi must serve a minimum of 20 years in prison before being eligible for parole and will be on the sex offenders register for life.

Once eligible for parole he will be on licence for eight years.

articles.title: Three US citizens among 4 convicted in Honduras over sex-trafficking case
articles.summary: The defendants face 10 years in jail after being found guilty of recruiting women into a sex-trafficking ring.
articles.body:
A court in Honduras has convicted four people, including three United States citizens, of criminal association in connection with the 2022 disappearance of a woman whose whereabouts are still unknown.

The Public Ministry said on Friday that it would request the maximum jail term of 10 years for each defendant after they were found guilty of recruiting women into a sex-trafficking ring. The next hearing is due to take place on December 9.

The ministry also said it would appeal the court’s decision to acquit US citizens Harold Green and William James Murdock of human trafficking.

They were found guilty of the lesser crime of criminal association, along with fellow US national Gary Lee Johnston and Honduran national Gustavo Trejo.

Angie Pena disappeared on January 1, 2022, while jet skiing by the Caribbean island of Roatan, off the northern coast of Honduras.

She was a 22-year-old university student when she went missing and police initially suspected she had drowned. However, her family believed she had been abducted and demanded an investigation.

A trafficking investigation was later launched after the jet ski Pena had used was found in Belize, about 90 nautical miles (170 kilometres) away from Roatan.

Investigators later found she had fallen prey to a sex-trafficking network called “Delta Teams” that has since been dismantled. The Attorney General’s Office determined minors were among the trafficked victims.

“The Public Ministry [Attorney General’s Office] obtained a guilty verdict against four members of the network known as Delta Teams for the violation of criminal association,” the prosecutor’s office said on X.

Three US nationals, identified as Harold Green, William Murdock and Gary Lee Johnston, as well as Honduran national Ramon Trejo, were found guilty of “locating, recruiting, and transporting women via social media”.

Green and Murdock were acquitted of human trafficking on Friday after the court concluded there was insufficient evidence to link them to Pena’s disappearance and alleged trafficking.

The case highlights the struggles women in Honduras face when seeking justice after being violently abused.

The country has a femicide rate of 4.3 cases per 100,000 inhabitants, the highest in Latin America, according to the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC).

Friday’s trial was not open to the public or media, prompting Pena’s family to question its transparency.

In August, a key protected witness was killed. Following his death, videos were released of Dereck McNeil, in which he accused a special unit in the public prosecutor’s office of corruption.

The ATIC denies it is corrupt and says it was not involved in investigating Pena’s disappearance.

“The ruling indicates to the Public Prosecutor’s Office that it must continue investigating, as the lines of inquiry in Angie Pena’s case have not been exhausted,” said Kenia Paz, a lawyer for the Legal Team for Human Rights, which represents Pena’s family.

“The ruling and what has been done so far by the state do not bring Angie Pena back. They do not tell us where she is, and that is what we need to know: what happened to Angie and when she will return.”

Pena’s aunt Yenely Diaz told the AFP news agency: “They told us it was an accident; everything was conducted through organised crime.”

articles.title: Birmingham's York Road named one of the coolest streets in the world
articles.summary: York Road in Kings Heath has been included in the Time Out list of coolest streets in the world.
articles.body:
It's the Birmingham street packed with independent shops and restaurants, has a legendary pub on the corner and a unique vibe.

York Road, in the lively suburb of Kings Heath, has been included in the Time Out list of coolest streets in the world , ranking alongside hipster hangouts in Bangkok, London and Buenos Aires.

Global entertainment magazine Time Out praised it for its "pub tables spilling across the street, colourful painted shop fronts and a buzzy community feel that's hard to come by in the city centre."

For Kings Heath resident Chloe Carpenter, who nominated the road for the accolade, it was the "fuzzy, community feel" that made it a hit, both among locals and visitors.

Carpenter, who has lived in Kings Heath for the last nine years, said she noticed Time Out had been looking for UK communities outside of London.

Her application included her thoughts on where to eat, drink and shop on the street, as well as a brief background on its history.

The renowned Hare & Hounds, a music venue and pub, has been pouring pints on the corner of York Road since 1907 and dates back to 1820.

The Grade II-listed building with its Art Nouveau tiles was the first place that Birmingham reggae band UB40 played and, along with the road's other music venues like Fletchers and Schooners, continues to keep the area's live scene bustling.

The picnic benches that line the pedestrianised street in all sorts of weather give York Road its al-fresco vibe, where kids regularly play while adults catch up with friends and even get up and dance.

Pete Bradbury has lived round the corner from York Road for 36 years and regularly enjoys what the street's hospitality businesses have to offer.

He agreed it is the atmosphere that the residents and visitors create that make it one of the coolest streets.

"There's good people round here, if it ain't for the people, it doesn't exist," Bradbury added.

Megan Haywood, 22, who works at the The Hare & Hounds but grew up in Shirley, Solihull, said she noticed a real difference in the sense of community when she moved to the area.

"In the year I lived here I'd walk down the road, speak to 10 people and know who they all are, it's just very comfortable and welcoming," she said.

The street's socialising scene is a result of the introduction of a traffic reduction scheme .

While some residents welcomed the Low Traffic Neighbourhood (LTN) with its creation of outdoor dining space and cycling friendly roads, others were left upset saying other roads had become "blocked" and turned into "a car park".

But the scheme has meant York Road can host community events including its own annual Pride event, where for one day Kings Heath becomes Queens Heath.

Thousands of people, dressed in bright colours and doused in glitter, flood the street for the day of festivities.

A Pride march gets the jam-packed day under way, with performers later taking to the stage outside The Hare & Hounds pub, meanwhile a famous face can often be spotted among the crowds, as Celebrity Traitors star and Brum comedian Joe Lycett, is one of the organisers.

Carpenter believes her nomination was "helped along" the mention of Lycett who lives nearby and often visits the The Hare & Hounds, which Time Out also named as the ninth best pub in the UK back in April.

Joe Cherry, who lives in nearby Stirchley, and regularly heads to the road said the street comes to life in the summer."

He credited the road's "London vibe" for its success and said on the long, light nights he often felt like he was in the capital but "without the hustle and bustle, and the price tag".

Scarlet Elwell, 22, who also works at The Hare & Hounds, said it was different compared to Birmingham's other social areas, such as Digbeth.

"The music we play, the variety, it's different every week," she added.

Adrian Davenport has lived in Kings Heath for more than 50 years and his partner Jane Elsden was born on what is now one of the world's coolest roads.

"According to my mom, I spent the first six months of my life in a little bedsit, or flat on York Road," Elsden said.

"It's phenomenal news [that it's been recognised]," she added.

Davenport said he had "always said they should have built a big arch here, like the one at the entrance to Carnaby Street in London".

John-Paul McCaughey, who owns Schooners, a craft beer bar on the road, joked it was normal to be compared to cities like Buenos Aires, Montreal and Bangkok.

"They're all kind of boring cities when you compare them to Brum," he said.

He hoped the recognition would bring more people to the area and called on those who had maybe not seen Birmingham as a "cool place" to give York Road a try.

"[They] don't know what they're missing out on, bigger is not always better."

articles.title: AI and social media allows memories of the lost to be preserved
articles.summary: With much of our lives lived online, preserving memories of people who have died is far easier now.
articles.body:
From voice notes and photographs to saved messages and AI (artificial intelligence) recreations, technology has enabled new ways for bereaved people to maintain connections with those they have lost.

But while digital memories might offer consolation, they can also make the grieving process more complicated, particularly when reminders resurface unexpectedly, some experts claim.

Karen Sutton, who provides support for bereaved people in her role as a widow coach based in Cheltenham, said: "There can come a point when things that once bought us comfort can actually be holding us back."

With our loved ones immortalised in the digital world - their likeness preserved and always accessible - has modern technology permanently altered the process of saying goodbye?

'I focused on getting a baby, not what came next'

Pontins fined £1m after grandmother's death

The process of grieving is unique to each person, Sutton said, meaning there is no universal formula for negotiating it.

"For some people, being able to access voice messages, having reminders on their phone or photos pop up will feel like a connection to their person," she added.

"They might even see them as signs, but for others, it might feel like torment."

Sutton said it is important people "check in with yourself" as grief evolves, making the any changes needed to move forward "without attaching too much meaning to things", such as cancelling anniversary reminders or deleting voicemails.

"If you find it comforting, then absolutely access it, use it, leave it as it is," she said.

"But if it's something that is impacting your pain in some way, find a way to stop that thing from happening."

With AI-generated content becoming increasingly prevalent, Sutton said she is worried people using it to fabricate "new memories" of loved ones could hinder the healing process.

"When somebody dies, your brain has to learn that your person no longer exists in this reality, and that takes a lot of time and rewiring," she said.

"When you create an AI version of your person, that would tell your brain that your person still exists in some form, and I don't know how helpful that is."

Prof Kate Woodthorpe is co-director for the world-leading research Centre of Death and Society at the University of Bath, and a specialist in grief and bereavement.

She said: "There are more digital remnants of a person's life online now than there ever has been, and we're still only at the start of technological revolution.

"By the time we get into the 2050s, people will have lived their whole lives online and there will be an enormous amount of content left behind when they die."

With everything still at our fingertips, Woodthorpe posed the question: "Do we ever really have to say goodbye?"

She emphasised that a reliance on these "digital legacies" will likely vary with age, as younger generations are typically more accustomed to constant connectivity than those who grew up without the internet.

But some people say technology has served as a vital outlet for their grief.

Kelsey Mulcahy, 33, began posting tributes to her late fiancé Joseph Day, who died in 2022 shortly after the couple moved from New Zealand to Bristol.

She has since amassed more than 45,000 followers on TikTok by sharing her honest experiences of bereavement and offering advice to others going through the same thing.

She previously told the BBC: "My community and the way that they message me and share their stories and tell me how much it's impacted them - that gives me so much meaning and purpose, which has made my grief so much easier to carry."

Katie Burnham and Natalie Krzak, from Surrey, met through the grief support website Widowed and Young (Way) after losing their husbands in December 2022.

Krzak said it enabled her to find a community when she needed it most, and described their first in-person meeting as a "defining moment in both of our grief journeys".

"To have that online space to connect to people who really understand the complexities of what you're going through is just incredible," she added.

"I was desperate to be truly honest about each and every emotion and thought I was experiencing, and to have that outlet translated into a genuine friendship was such a positive at a time of such turmoil."

The women have since launched a podcast called Those Two Widows, where they share honest accounts of navigating grief in your 30s.

"Sharing our lives in this way on the internet isn't always easy, but we're firm believers in honest conversations," added Burnham.

"The digital space has provided an amazing platform to share our experiences and also educate those who perhaps don't understand what life after loss can be like.

"We have received messages from so many widows and widowers in similar situations and feel immensely privileged and proud to be able to provide them with an outlet for their stories."

So how have social media platforms adapted to the modern process of grieving?

Facebook and Instagram allow users to convert loved ones' profiles into memorialised accounts, where people can share tributes.

Content that the person posted remains online and visible to the audience it was shared with, alongside keeping it secure by preventing anyone from logging in.

But if the digital reminders are too painful, families with the documentation such as a death certificate may request the removal of accounts on TikTok and X.

Facebook also offers the option to hide memories involving specific people or within a particular date range, while Instagram users can filter names or phrases.

articles.title: How the Molineux inspired a photographer who dislikes football
articles.summary: Ian Hughes' photographs of the stadium feature in an exhibition at Wolverhampton's Central Library.
articles.body:
A photographer who admits he has no interest in football visited the home of Wolverhampton Wanderers for his new exhibition.

Despite describing himself as someone who dislikes football Ian Hughes said he was instead fascinated by Molineux's architecture and the history behind the club.

"I'm recording Wolverhampton," he said. "The two are intrinsically linked, I think."

"I was invited in and allowed to photograph pretty much anything I wanted."

Hughes was invited to the ground after asking whether he could get access through his Celebrating Wolverhampton group on Facebook.

Hughes, who lives in Pendeford and has created numerous photography exhibitions, such as his remembrance exhibition in the city's Central Library , visited the ground in March.

He was escorted by club historian Peter Crump, who oversees the museum collection and archives.

"I was allowed to just go around and look at it from an architectural point of view and just get views of the stand," he said.

"It's got an interest to me on the history and the background and stories of individual players. That interests me."

The exhibition features photographs taken from both inside and outside the stadium, including shots of the stands, the pitch and seating areas, as well various memorabilia and artefacts.

The photos of the exterior were taken over the course of about a year, with the interior taken during a one-day visit to the stadium.

"Some [photos that] seem to have caught the attraction of many is the back of Billy Wright's boot," he said of the exhibition.

"People have said that's odd, because rather than taking a photo of Billy Wright, although I do have one, I found the picture of the sole of the foot, just his boot... because apparently there's only six studs and nobody plays with six studs anymore."

Hughes, originally from Aberystwyth in Wales, said despite not being a Wolves fan, he had also written a poem celebrating the club.

"I want positivity. I'm tired of people saying that Wolverhampton's a dump and so on because it really isn't," he said.

Wolves ay we? Molineux: Heart of the pack, is running on the first floor of the library until 8 January, coinciding with the club's upcoming 150 year anniversary in 2027.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Pakistan's minister Musadik Malik expressed a desire to visit some of India's heritage sites, including the iconic Taj Mahal.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Pakistan's minister Musadik Malik expressed a desire to visit some of India's heritage sites, including the iconic Taj Mahal. Malik attended the SCO meeting in New Delhi as part of the Shehbaz Sharif-led government.His visit marks the first by a Pakistani minister to India since then-foreign minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari's high-profile visit in 2023 for the SCO meeting.Accompanied by his wife and a senior Pakistani official, Malik spoke about his interest in exploring India beyond the multilateral engagement. Both are visiting India for the first time.Asked whether he planned to visit the Taj Mahal and explore other parts of the country, Malik said he hoped to meet people and see some places if his schedule allowed."I have come to India for a few days. Tomorrow I will be engaged due to the SCO forum. I may not be able to explore much this time, but whatever opportunity I will get, I will try to meet people also and see some places, and understand them. People are the same everywhere," he said.The Centre, meanwhile, denied imposing any restrictions on the movement of Malik or other ministers attending the event. Official sources said all visiting ministers were free to travel anywhere in the country, including the Taj Mahal and Humayun's Tomb. However, security considerations may have affected the possibility of Malik visiting the Hazrat Nizamuddin Dargah.Speaking on the sidelines of the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum at the historic Purana Qila, Malik was also asked whether the multilateral engagement could help improve India-Pakistan relations.He said he had come to India for discussions in a multilateral context, while underlining the importance of cultural exchanges in bringing people and countries closer."This forum is itself multilateral. You should engage in multilateral discussions. Even the questions you have asked today have not been bilateral; everything here is happening in a multilateral context. We have also come here for multilateral discussions," he said.Amid continued unease in bilateral ties following the April 22, 2025, Pahalgam terror attack, which claimed 26 lives, Malik said culture had a "key role" to play in fostering dialogue between the two countries.He stressed that cultural engagement was not limited to bilateral relations but had wider regional significance, adding that greater understanding between people was essential for the region's progress."Unless we understand each other, our way of thinking and manners of living, we won't be able to grow. Through dialogues, we will get each other's perspectives and get to know each other's understanding, and that's how the region will be able to grow," the Pakistan minister said.India-Pakistan ties deteriorated further in April 2025 after Pakistan-backed terrorists killed 26 people in an attack in south Kashmir's Pahalgam. articles.body: A province-wide shutdown was observed in Quetta and several districts of Pakistan's Balochistan province on Thursday after the All parties alliance called for a protest against worsening law and order, rising inflation, unemployment and prolonged power and gas shortages, Dawn reported.Markets, shops and commercial establishments remained closed in several parts of the province. articles.title: Trafalgar Square Christmas tree sets off from Oslo to London
articles.summary: The 21m tree is Oslo’s annual thank you for Britain’s support during World War Two.
articles.body:
This year's Trafalgar Square Christmas tree has been cut down in a forest outside Oslo, ready to begin its journey to London.

The 21m (69ft) tree, nicknamed Jolly Cheery, is about 75 years old. It was felled on Friday by the Lord Mayor of Westminster, Karen Scarborough, and the Mayor of Oslo, Anne Lindboe.

Norway has sent a tree to the capital every year since 1947 as a thank you for Britain's support during World War Two, when King Haakon VII and the Norwegian government lived in exile in London.

Its lights will be switched on by the two mayors at a ceremony in the square on Thursday, 3 December.

Scarborough said: "It's my greatest honour to take part in this wonderful tradition for both the cities of Oslo and London.

"This tree is a powerful symbol of friendship and peace, reminding us to be there for one another during the festive period."

Scarborough thanked "the people of Oslo and Norway for this truly fabulous gift" and added: "With the care and dedication of the team, I'm sure it will look magnificent on Trafalgar Square."

Lindboe said: "Oslo has been sending a Christmas tree to London for almost eight decades, and every year we send a tree across the North Sea with the same message: we have not forgotten.

"The tradition has a powerful history, and its message remains just as relevant today.

"I hope Jolly Cheery spreads warmth and Christmas cheer to everyone who passes by, and reminds us how much it means to be there for one another, especially in difficult times."

For the second year running, the tree was chosen with the help of a social media poll.

Organisers said it would travel by road in Norway and England using only electric and biodiesel vehicles, cutting the journey's carbon footprint by 80%. It will cross the North Sea on a regular cargo ship from the port of Brevik.

Once in London, it will be decorated in the traditional Norwegian style, with 25m strings of festoon lighting fitted with energy-efficient bulbs.

articles.title: In Cambodia’s Kep waters, conservationists installed interlocking concrete blocks to snag trawler nets; the barriers reduced patrol needs, saving an estimated 500,000 litres of fuel a year
articles.summary: Learn how innovative interlocking concrete blocks are transforming marine conservation efforts in Cambodia, reducing illegal fishing and saving fuel while supporting local communities.
articles.body: Off the coast of Kep in Cambodia, a low-cost idea is helping protect the seabed. According to the Asian Development Bank’s Southeast Asia Development Solutions team, conservationists have installed interlocking concrete blocks that snag the nets of illegal bottom trawlers. With the barriers, the need for patrols has been reduced, saving around 500,000 litres of fuel per year. It was a simple idea with a big goal: helping fish and the families that depend on them bounce back.Why Cambodia’s coast needed a handFishing is a big part of life in Cambodia. The Asian Development Bank says the industry contributes 8% to 10% of the country's GDP and provides a livelihood for millions of people. Fish is also the most commonly consumed food in the country after rice. However, the bank’s research shows that the fish stock experienced a dramatic decline of about 40% to 60% between 2017 and 2022. It blames overfishing as well as mangrove loss and the deterioration of seabeds, the latter largely due to bottom trawling. Without stronger coastal and marine ecosystems, the bank predicts stocks could drop by a further 30% by 2030.How the blocks work Since 2018, Cambodia's Fisheries Administration has been working with Marine Conservation Cambodia, a community-based group, to place large passive structures in the sea. The group came up with modular concrete and rebar blocks that were low-cost and easy to build. They were built and placed by local communities, with the blocks assembled underwater to form a complete structure. The structures mark the edge of a marine protected area and act as barriers against illegal bottom trawling. The nets of trawling vessels get caught on them, discouraging illegal fishing. The blocks do more than just stop nets. They also create an artificial reef and habitat for young fish. In Kep, they were seeded with locally grown oyster spat, which gave the community another income source and helped filter the water. The work also helped protect the habitats of endangered species such as the Irrawaddy dolphin, dugong, sea turtles and seahorses.What the research shows A 2025 Frontiers in Marine Science paper by Amanda Ho and team looked at the area in detail. According to the study, researchers surveyed an area of 62,146 hectares in four zones during the dry seasons of 2022 and 2023. Outside the protected Kep marine fisheries management area, seagrass was found only in shallow waters out of reach of trawlers. Within the protected zone, where the structures were in place, seagrass thrived in deeper areas. Halophila, a pioneer seagrass genus, was abundant near the blocks, hinting at regrowth. The authors saw it as an early sign of recovery. In Kampot, a neighbouring survey zone with no structures, Ho and colleagues noted that seagrass cover fell by 39% from 2013 to 2023. The authors worked for Marine Conservation Cambodia and said future studies should directly measure trawling activity.Plans to scale up In December 2022, the bank approved a $73 million financing package for Cambodia's marine fisheries, which included support for deploying more of these structures. France’s Agence Française de Développement was also set to provide co-financing equivalent to $20 million on top of that, administered by the bank. The project covered four coastal provinces: Kampot, Kep, Koh Kong and Preah Sihanouk. The idea was to place 5,000 structures in almost 40% of the near-shore fishery. The blocks would be made by the local community under a wage-for-work programme. The project would also support sustainable mariculture and business incubators for small firms, especially women-led ones. It was expected to benefit nearly 20,000 households and a wider coastal community of around 200,000 people. articles.title: A 10-year-old girl hid a handwritten letter beneath a staircase in 1982; 44 years later, a renovation worker found it and social media helped trace her within an hour
articles.summary: A house renovation in the English village of Hockley has brought an unexpected piece of family history back into view.
articles.body: A house renovation in the English village of Hockley has brought an unexpected piece of family history back into view. Tucked away beneath a staircase was a handwritten letter, left there in August 1982 by a 10-year-old girl who wanted someone in the future to find it. The paper remained hidden for 44 years, until a worker came across it while carrying out work at the property. The homeowner, Michelle Harwood, decided to share the discovery online, hoping to identify the child who had written it. Within an hour, social media users had helped reunite the letter with its author, now a 54-year-old teacher.What the 10-year-old girl wrote in her hidden 1982 letterThe discovery happened at Harwood's home in Hockley, a village in Essex, roughly 40 miles east of London. During renovation work, a tradesperson found a folded piece of paper concealed beneath the stairs and handed it to the homeowner.When Harwood opened it, she realised that it was not an ordinary note left behind by a previous occupant. It had been deliberately placed there decades earlier. The writer had addressed it to whoever might eventually come across it, explaining that it had been hidden on 12 August 1982, during the reign of Queen Elizabeth II.The letter also contained a short introduction to the person who had written it. She gave her name as Rachel North and described living in the house with her parents, brother and a cat named Kizzy. She included her date of birth, 11 February, and mentioned that she had been born in Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk.Harwood decided to photograph the handwritten message and post it in a local Facebook group. She wanted to find out whether the girl named in the letter could still be traced.The 10-year-old girl behind the 1982 letter is finally identifiedThe search did not take long. People familiar with the family recognised the name and began tagging the woman they believed had written the note. Within approximately an hour of Harwood's post, the online community had connected her with Rachel North, who is now known as Rachel Miles.Miles, 54, lives in Milton Keynes, around 85 miles from the house where she had left the letter. She responded to the Facebook post herself, confirming that the handwriting and message belonged to her. Her reply included a light-hearted question about whether anyone had also found the money she jokingly suggested she might have buried alongside the note.Her brother, Mike North, also joined the conversation. He recalled his sister hiding the letter and confirmed that the discovery had brought back memories from their childhood. He joked that he had been left out of the message, which mentioned their parents and the family cat but made no reference to him.What inspired Rachel Miles to hide a letter beneath the staircaseSpeaking to the BBC, Miles explained that the idea had come from the popularity of time capsules during the 1980s. The BBC children's programme Blue Peter had helped make the concept familiar to young viewers, encouraging children to preserve small pieces of the present for people to discover years later.Miles remembered that her father had found the space beneath the staircase. She then decided to use it as a hiding place for a letter addressed to someone who might come across it in the future.She had no particular recipient in mind. The idea was simply to leave behind a record of who she was at that point in her life, including details about her family and the household in which she lived.Speaking to the broadcaster, Miles said she was delighted that someone had eventually discovered the message. She also described the experience as a lovely opportunity to revisit her childhood, particularly after seeing comments from people who remembered her from the time she lived in the area.A 1982 handwritten letter gives homeowner goosebumpsFor Harwood, finding the letter was unexpected enough, but identifying its author so quickly made the experience even more unusual. She told the BBC that reading a message which had remained hidden for longer than she had been alive gave her goosebumps.She had initially posted the photograph without knowing whether anyone would recognise the name Rachel North. The response from local residents exceeded her expectations, with people helping to establish the writer's identity and reconnect the discovery with the family.Harwood also spoke about the role of social media in bringing people together, saying that the number of people connected through local online groups had made the search possible.The letter had spent more than four decades out of sight, surviving successive years inside the same property. Its discovery during routine renovation work eventually brought its writer back into contact with a place she had left behind as a child.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available reports.
