articles.title: French police officers guilty of Michel Zecler assault: What happens now?
articles.summary: Officers dealt more than 30 blows to the Black music producer in what the court ruled was a racially motivated crime.
articles.body:
A French court has found three French police officers guilty of intentional, racist violence during the 2020 assault of Michel Zecler , a Black music producer, and sentenced them to prison.

The landmark ruling has once again shone a spotlight on the issue of police brutality in France, which activists say is rarely prosecuted despite being systemic and often racially motivated.

Here’s what happened in the case and what it means now:

The Paris criminal court convicted three police officers of assaulting Zecler in Paris in 2020, ruling that the attack was racially motivated. The court also found the defendants guilty of falsifying a police report about the incident.

The officers – 29-year-old Aurelien Lapersonne, 50-year-old Philippe Tondeux and 37-year-old Pierre Plantier – were each sentenced to five years in prison, part of which was suspended.

All three have been barred from serving in the police force again.

Zecler is a 47-year-old French music producer who co-founded the independent rap label Black Gold Corp. Zecler has worked in the French hip-hop industry for years, including helping to put together the prominent 2016 rap tour called L’Age d’Or du Rap Francais.

Music journalist Olivier Cachin described Zecler as easy-going and humble. “He just works, staying very much in the background,” Cachin told French newspaper Sud Ouest. “He’s not a ‘look-at-me’ type… He’s just a big teddy bear.”

Why was Zecler beaten by the French police?

Officers stopped Zecler outside his Paris music studio on November 21, 2020, accusing him of failing to put on a compulsory face mask, as required by France’s COVID-19 restrictions at the time.

The officers then pushed Zecler back into the building and assaulted him – an incident captured by his security cameras.

Over five minutes or so, the officers punched, kicked and used batons to deliver some 30 blows to Zecler, severely injuring him. He suffered head trauma and a complete rupture of his biceps tendon.

Zecler said the officers repeatedly used a racist slur during the beating, and that the assault had left him “completely devastated”.

Officers Lapersonne, Paltier and Tondeux were found guilty of aggravated group assault that was racially motivated.

They were also convicted of falsifying an official police report in which they accused Zecler of being violent towards them – claims unsupported by the security footage.

The presiding judge said the officers had been dishonest in their report “to shield (themselves) from disciplinary and legal consequences, with no regard for the criminal consequences faced by Michel Zecler”.

Officer Lapersonne, who submitted the report, initially claimed that Zecler had attacked the officers and “struck out with his arms and legs”. When the presiding judge asked if he had “made that up”, Lapersonne responded during the trial, “Absolutely.” Lapersonne’s initial police report also failed to mention that the officers landed blows on Zecler.

“I deliberately omitted them. I think out of fear. It was stupid of me,” Lapersonne told the court.

All three of the convicted officers admitted to having used excessive force and apologised to Zecler, though they denied the charges of racism.

Tondeux, the oldest of the officers, said he regretted “the image I have given of the police”.

The judges said Zecler’s testimony, in which he claimed to have heard one of the officers use the racial slur “sale negre”, had been consistent from the beginning, while the officers’ falsified report damaged their credibility.

Speaking to the court, Zecler said he would likely not have been recognised as a victim if not for the security footage recording the incident.

How long have the French police officers been sentenced to prison?

All three were given five-year sentences, but with varying portions suspended.

Lapersonne, who was found to have first stopped Zecler and authored the falsified police report, had three years of his sentence suspended, while Tondeux had three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended and will serve the remaining year under electronic monitoring rather than in prison.

Zecler’s lawyer described the sentences as “falling short”, but said they set an important precedent.

“This precedent shows that even if a police officer lies, someone who comes forward to say the police did the worst to them can be believed,” said the lawyer.

What does the Michel Zecler case reveal about police brutality in France?

Zecler’s case is the latest to draw attention to the issue of police brutality in France, which is rarely prosecuted, as well as racial discrimination, following several high-profile cases in recent years.

In 2023, protests and riots broke out after Nahel Merzouk , a 17-year-old boy of North African descent, was shot and killed by a police officer during a traffic stop outside Paris. Police initially reported that an officer had shot at him because the teenager was driving his car at him, but this version of events was contradicted by a video circulating on social media. In March, a French appeals court ruled that the officer who shot Merzouk should stand trial.

In 2024, a judge handed suspended prison sentences to three officers who caused permanent rectal injuries to a Black man, Theo Luhaka , during a stop-and-search in 2017.

In 2016, Adama Traore, a 24-year-old man of Malian descent, died in custody after being restrained and apprehended by police following a dispute over an identity check. A case against three arresting police officers was dropped in 2023 and, in February this year, France’s top court, the Court of Cassation, ruled against reopening the investigation.

A 2025 report published by France’s Defender of Rights (Defenseur des droits), led by Claire Hedon, found that young men “perceived as Arab, black or from North Africa” are four times more likely to be stopped under police stop-and-search powers than the overall population.

They are also 12 times more likely to be subjected to more severe measures, such as being frisked during checks, the report found.

The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) also condemned France last year for identity checks it deemed “discriminatory” following a case brought by six French citizens of African or North African origin.

Will the issue of police brutality be addressed in France?

France is coming under increasing pressure to address this issue.

The country was rocked by protests in September against proposed legislation that would grant additional protections to law enforcement officials using firearms in the line of duty.

The new law, which the French Senate is currently considering, will grant police officers a “licence to kill”, critics say.

“It’s a very dangerous piece of legislation. It’s liberticide,” Rim-Sarah Alouane, a legal scholar and an associate researcher in public law at the University of Toulouse Capitole, told Al Jazeera . “It would create a sense of impunity amongst police officers – which already exists, but this would strengthen that. It would undermine investigations and make access to the justice system even more difficult for victims and their families.

“It raises serious issues regarding equality under the law because it puts a presumption of innocence in favour of people because of their profession as cops.”

But while French officials have acknowledged isolated cases of police misconduct, they have so far pushed back against claims of systemic racism or discrimination by law enforcement.

In 2023, Laurent Nunez, then prefect of the Paris police, said “there is no racism in the police force.”

Activists say the French authorities’ refusal to address the institutional nature of police brutality further endangers minorities.

“The people who are dying are mostly Black or Arab,” French activist Assa Traore, the sister of Adama Traore, said in an interview with the Anadolu news agency earlier this year. “Admitting that racism exists is not a weakness. It’s about saving lives.”

Alouane said that Zecler’s case was obviously “about institutional racism, systemic discrimination and police violence”.

“Everything is connected. Not only are we dealing with police violence against a Black man, but that’s on top of attempting to conceal evidence and falsify a report,” said Alouane. “When these reports are falsified, we’re questioning the integrity of the entire system.”

articles.title: FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
articles.summary: The National Crime Information Center database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information.
articles.body:
The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media report citing two people briefed on the issue.

The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks. The BBC has contacted the FBI for comment.

This comes after string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyberattacks - but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.

White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with US President Donald Trump saying he was not good enough.

It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US.

In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.

After that hack, one former FBI agent told the BBC he feared for the safety of current employees, whose personal information could soon become available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.

In a separate development, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) .

Employees were informed on Thursday that its farm payment system had been targeted, NBC said.

The USDA has not publicly commented on the issue.

articles.title: Nations agree to ‘elaborate’ on rules for AI-run ‘killer robots’ by 2028
articles.summary: Members of the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons fail to agree on swift adoption of legally binding rules.
articles.body:
The 128 countries at a United Nations conference in the Swiss city of Geneva have agreed to “elaborate” on a possible accord regulating lethal autonomous weapons, known as “killer robots”, in the next two years.

Saturday’s announcement at the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) came after nearly 100 nations pushed for swift adoption of legally binding rules on the weapons capable of killing without a human making the final decision to fire.

Key arms-producing nations, including the United States, Russia and Israel, opposed the push. Decisions under the convention require the agreement of all member states.

Diplomats said Russia’s objections over procedure led to some formal sessions being called off. Talks over the final wording then ran through the night.

Julien Thoeni, the Swiss diplomat who chaired the conference, said some countries had rejected the word “negotiate”. The agreed text refers instead to the “elaboration” of an instrument.

He said more than 10 years of talks had produced a significant step for humanitarian disarmament.

“It shows that even in today’s deeply divided world, multilateral diplomacy can still deliver concrete results,” he told reporters as the meeting wrapped up.

He said the process should determine which weapons can be banned under international humanitarian law and which can be permitted but regulated.

Stop Killer Robots, a coalition of 300 organisations opposed to the development and use of autonomous weapons, called the mandate “watered down”, saying it offered no clear route to legally binding rules.

Its executive director, Nicole van Rooijen, said autonomous weapons were being deployed in combat, including systems that use artificial intelligence to choose targets.

“Delaying the creation of a legally binding instrument puts civilians and humanity at risk,” she told the AFP news agency.

Verity Coyle, deputy director for arms at Human Rights Watch, said the outcome was disappointing.

“It does not provide the urgent action needed to agree new rules – but the technology is racing ahead,” she told AFP.

articles.title: Russian missiles hit Poland: What happened, and could NATO respond?
articles.summary: Warsaw accuses Moscow of intentional provocation, but bar for triggering NATO’s collective defence clause remains high.
articles.body:
Security cameras captured the moment a suspected Russian missile struck Polish territory during an attack on Ukraine on Friday. Poland’s government says it may have been hit by two missiles and a jet-powered drone.

The incident, which took place as European troops held military drills in the country and as the United States pushes to revive talks on ending the war in Ukraine, have raised questions about whether the strike was deliberate.

So what happened, and does this mean Russia has struck Poland, a NATO member?

Poland’s Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told a news conference in Warsaw that two missiles and a jet-powered drone fell on Polish territory during Russia’s overnight attack on November 20. The missiles came down at Nowy Lipowiec and Rudnik nad Sanem, while the jet-powered drone fell at Molodycz, all in the country’s southeast.

One missile is believed to have crashed about 35km (22 miles) from where European troops’ military exercises were taking place. A Kh-101 cruise missile went down about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border, and what officials believe was a jet-powered drone hit about 30km (20 miles) from the border. No immediate injuries or damage were reported.

That night, Russia launched one of its heaviest bombardments of Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia fired more than 400 drones and at least 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles, some with cluster warheads. At least eight civilians were killed and more than two dozen were wounded.

Why did a Russian missile enter Polish airspace?

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it appeared “we are dealing with an intentional provocation” by Russia. He said the incident was likely timed to coincide with the European military exercises in Poland. The unprecedented two-week exercise began on November 9 in southeastern Poland and is preparing forces for a possible post-war mission in Ukraine to help stabilise the country and rebuild its military.

Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at the Clinton Institute, University College Dublin, told Al Jazeera that the incident “fits into a pattern going back for months” of Russia “testing how far they can go”.

“A few months ago, it was flying the drones into airspace , and indeed a couple of times they flew fighter jets across the border into the Baltic states,” he said. “You just test how NATO responds.”

This time, he said, Moscow had “gone a bit further”. “You lob a couple of missiles across and a drone” near where 11 countries are holding exercises.

The Polish Air Force had launched preventive air patrols on September 17 aimed at securing the eastern part of Polish airspace following repeated incursions in the previous weeks.

Harry Nedelcu, partner and senior director for geopolitics at Rasmussen Global, said the testing has not been limited to Poland.

“During the war, there’s been repeated instances of Russia testing NATO allies – Poland, Romania and also non-NATO Moldova as well, which is experiencing – especially over the last few months – increasing numbers of drones and missiles flying over its territory and airspace,” he told Al Jazeera.

He linked the incursions to one of Moscow’s core war aims. “One of the key goals in Ukraine that Russia has had in the full-scale invasion, that has lasted almost five years now, has been to prevent Ukraine from being a part of NATO,” he said. “So their goal clearly is to undermine NATO, to do everything possible to undermine it.

“What Russia is doing with these missiles, drones, that sometimes find their way into NATO territory, tests NATO just under the radar of Article 5 to see how far can they push things. How far can they take hybrid warfare?”

Under Article 5 , each member of the NATO alliance understands that if one of them is the “victim of an armed attack, each and every other member of the alliance will consider this act of violence as an armed attack against all members”.

At a meeting on Thursday with European leaders in Germany’s capital, Berlin, US President Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner said he believes Russia would be “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for post-war Ukraine.

Kushner and fellow special envoy Steve Witkoff have been holding talks with Ukraine and Russia in recent days, in a push for peace which has been viewed as sidelining Ukraine’s European allies.

Following the Berlin meeting, French President Emmanuel Macron said Ukraine’s membership of NATO should be considered again, prompting Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov to push back.

Ryabkov said any form of “quasi membership” for Kyiv of the Western ‌military alliance was totally unacceptable for Moscow, Russian state media reported.

Lucas said the timing of the missile incursion into Polish territory now is very likely tied to the ongoing US-led peace talks.

“The Russians cannot be seen to go through talks and completely exclude Europe,” he said. He described the Kremlin’s push for a “Europe-wide security architecture” as a way to avoid discussing a ceasefire or security guarantees for Ukraine.

“Rather than having a strong Europe at the talks, they want to try to divide Europe, they want to try to unsettle Europe, they want to try to scare Europe,” he said.

He also pointed to Ukraine’s recent strikes on the Kerch Bridge , which links occupied Crimea to Russia. He said these were seen as “a very serious attack on Russian capabilities” with “severe political, military and economic consequences”.

The latest Russian bombardment follows President Vladimir Putin’s pledge to retaliate against those strikes.

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called the missile incident a “grave violation” of Poland’s airspace. On X, he said the incident was “clearly dangerous” and a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine. Rutte is expected to visit Poland this weekend.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham called it “utterly unacceptable”. Germany’s Foreign Ministry called it “yet another example of Russia’s ongoing provocations”.

US President Donald Trump had played down earlier incursions hours before. “Putin has been landing drones in Poland and a couple of little missiles, by mistake,” he said.

Nedelcu said Warsaw’s reaction was “definitely a strong one”, with Polish officials “drawing a parallel between the fact that actually around the same time there were exercises by the Coalition of the Willing [those countries willing to provide support to Ukraine] nearby, and that this may have not been a coincidence”.

He said Poland is now “asking for more NATO support under this Eastern Sentry mission that already exists”.

“It’s not if, but what form that additional support will take – maybe an airborne early warning aircraft, or something of the sort,” he said.

“But what they have stopped short of is invoking Article 4,” he added, referring to the clause under which allies consult each other before invoking Article 5. “It’s unclear whether this was at their own volition. Maybe perhaps allies don’t want to use it too often, because Article 4 is also quite serious. It has been invoked not often, and it loses its value if it’s constantly invoked.”

Lucas said the public condemnation from European leaders was itself the message to Moscow. “It’s a signal to the Russians: look, we know what you’re doing, we see what you’re doing here,” he said.

“But you’re not going to run it up into an all-out military confrontation over a couple of missiles.”

He said he expects the response to be “defensive”, built on “preparedness” of ground forces, air, naval and cyber-defence, and defence against disinformation. “These will be the most intense preparations you will have had, certainly since the 1980s and possibly well before that,” he said.

On the same day, Denmark took action on a separate front. It announced that it was expelling Russia’s defence attache after Danish intelligence concluded that Moscow had orchestrated a plot to assassinate Ukrainian-American rapper Kyivstoner during a concert near Copenhagen.

Could a Russian missile strike on Poland trigger NATO’s Article 5?

Probably not. Article 5 treats an attack on any ally as an attack on all 32 members, but invoking it is a political decision requiring agreement from all members, not an automatic trigger. Poland can instead invoke Article 4, which provides for emergency consultations only. Warsaw did so in September 2025, after Russian drones entered its airspace.

Lucas said NATO members want to stop Russia succeeding in Ukraine without allowing the conflict to escalate. “[That] means you set a very high bar for invoking Article 5,” he said.

“You’re talking about what in effect would be a sustained Russian attack on Poland. That’s when Article 5 gets invoked.”

He said NATO is also handling a delicate diplomatic moment. US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are pressing for a negotiated settlement, and “NATO can’t be seen to be the ones to sabotage the talks”.

Those talks remain murky, particularly after Kushner’s comments indicating that Russia would be “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for post-war Ukraine.

“Jared Kushner is going around making statements that make absolutely no sense about what deal is on the table,” Lucas said. He said the US is “so desperate for a deal” that it is “muddying the waters”.

Lucas said Ukraine has no real prospect of NATO membership now, because “bringing Ukraine into NATO would destabilise a ceasefire”. He said the goal should be “security guarantees as if Ukraine was a NATO member”.

Could the incident escalate the Russia-Ukraine war?

Analysts say a direct confrontation between Russia and NATO is unlikely for now.

“The alliance shows every signal that it does not want to show any teeth,” Nedelcu said. “So what will probably happen, Russia will keep on testing the alliance. We should not expect that this is the last instance of this.

“The alliance is not trying to show Russia, you know, enough is enough, so Russia will still keep testing because they want to see where that threshold is,” he said.

Lucas said the bigger danger is a wider campaign of hybrid, or “grey zone”, warfare, including cyberattacks and disinformation, rather than direct strikes. “That’s where the real threat here is right now, rather than direct Russian strikes,” he said.

“I’m not going to say that it couldn’t escalate at some point, because you always have unintended escalation,” he added. “But I don’t want to go to the headlines and say this is it, World War III.”

Inside Ukraine, Nedelcu said, the war is intensifying in the air rather than on the ground. He described the incident in Poland as “a residual, if you will, collateral of the conflict in Ukraine”.

“On the front line, the conflict in Ukraine is pretty much static,” he said. “But what happens in Ukraine is that the air attack has been increasingly amplified, I would say, since the end of the summer.

“Russia is trying to essentially make Ukrainian cities especially unliveable – destroying its energy grid, trying to undermine even water supply, bridges, railways, logistics – in order to, if they cannot break it on the front lines, break it economically and break its civilian population.”

Lucas said any offensive pressure on Moscow would come through Ukraine’s own counterattacks, which he said Europe and NATO back, but the Trump administration does not.

“The more that you limit Russia’s capacity by hitting its refineries, its chemical plants, its engineering plants, by hitting the bridges, the more you increase the pressure on the Russians to try to stop the invasion,” he said.

articles.title: Havana film posters printed during blackouts go on show in London
articles.summary: Rare posters printed through blackouts and shortages go on show in London.
articles.body:
Film posters hand-printed in Havana through months of blackouts have gone on show in London.

The 11 silkscreen prints were made by the poster workshop of ICAIC, Cuba's national film institute, for the recent London Latino Film Festival, which ran in October.

The team had planned 25 designs, but power cuts, water shortages and a lack of materials meant the work dragged on for months and only 11 were finished.

"We can't do anything without power," said master printer Markito Guerra Rojas. "Number one, we can't see. Number two, the materials start to go wrong."

According to the workshop in Havana, they were printed in black, white and red because those were the only inks available, and were sent to London wrapped in a cement bag to protect them on the journey.

Guerra Rojas and his four-person team, who have worked in the same Havana workshop for 20 years, spent much of the year working to the rhythm of the power grid.

"A neighbour would let us know the power had come back, we'd start printing, and the power would go again," he said.

"Sometimes we had to stay, because how were we going to leave in that darkness?"

Cuba has faced severe fuel shortages since January, when the US cut off oil shipments from Venezuela and threatened tariffs on any country supplying the island. Most of its electricity is generated from oil, and the workshop said some neighbourhoods went close to a week without power in the summer.

The UN has said the restrictions are harming ordinary Cubans, while the US State Department has blamed the blackouts on mismanagement by the Cuban government.

For the printers, it also meant hunting for supplies. "There used to be companies that imported them. Now nobody does," Guerra Rojas said.

Silkscreen printing, or serigraphy, is done by hand, with ink pushed through fine mesh on a frame one colour at a time. Each colour needs its own screen, its own hand-mixed ink and its own drying time.

The photographic emulsion that fixes each design to its screen spoils when the electricity goes, and without power the press loses the suction that holds the paper flat.

"Something we might have done in a month, because while one colour was drying we could have been printing the next, we couldn't do," he said. "We'd do one colour and finish it, and then there was no power to prepare the screen for the next colour. It was catastrophic."

ICAIC was set up in 1959, months after the Cuban revolution. Its publicity department, led by Saúl Yelín, decided film posters should be works of design rather than advertising. The method began as a necessity and became a national art form, as central to Cuban cinema as the films themselves.

With no box office to chase, designers made posters for everything from Soviet dramas to Hollywood westerns, each built around a single bold idea in a few flat colours.

Silkscreen suited a country short of industrial presses too, and it is still how the posters are made. Guerra Rojas believes his may be the only workshop in the world still screen-printing posters to promote films.

Some of these posters are now recognised internationally as important cultural heritage, with the 1960–1980 collection inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2023. It's also the first time the posters have been made for an event abroad.

He does not see the reduced edition as a defeat.

"You depend on one thing, then another, then another to get there," he said. "That's also where the value of serigraphy lies: in the way it's made."

Irinka Cordovi, who heads the workshop, said she hoped visitors who see the exhibition "feel the same admiration we feel for these works of art, because they really are true works of art, and that they value them, admire them and enjoy them".

They are on display in Eclectic Gallery until 9 December.

articles.title: Princess of Wales: Catherine talks about her cancer journey in new documentary Heal
articles.summary: "There is a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you," says Catherine in the documentary.
articles.body:
The Princess of Wales has spoken about how "cancer does change you," in a forthcoming documentary called Heal to be shown on the BBC.

"It changes your body, it changes you physically - but there is a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you," says Catherine in the first glimpses from the documentary, which features her private thoughts on her illness and recovery.

The highly personal film, to be screened on BBC One on 29 November, will see Catherine share her experiences of cancer, saying: "Healing is a journey."

It includes new footage of her completing the Three Peaks Challenge earlier this year, which involved climbing the highest peaks in England, Scotland and Wales over a day.

"It's clear we're not meant to carry life's challenges alone," says Catherine's voice-over, accompanied by images of other cancer patients and the princess hugging her own family, including Prince William.

"It is often through pain that we realise there is a greater beauty that lies beyond that," she says, once again reflecting the sense of change from her cancer experience.

Catherine has never disclosed what type of cancer she faced, but in March 2024 she revealed that she had a diagnosis of cancer and was receiving chemotherapy .

In January 2025 she announced that she was in remission and in the following months began a gradual return to royal duties.

She has often spoken about her different understanding of life after her illness, and the need to take a more holistic approach to well-being beyond physical recovery.

The princess has talked about the good days and bad days that followed her treatment - and wanted to dispel the idea that patients could immediately return to how they felt before their illness.

This documentary, which will be introduced by Kirsty Young, promises to be the fullest and most personal account of that journey, with her own insights into the impact such illness can have and how she found her own healing process.

She has since returned to working for her charities and earlier this week was in India for the Earthshot Prize ceremony with Prince William, the first time they had travelled together on overseas royal duties since the princess's cancer treatment.

Among the film crew for the documentary, as director of photography, was Will Warr, who has worked with Catherine and her family before.

The filmmaker also made the personal video statement that marked the end of her chemotherapy in September 2024, with her message: "Out of darkness, can come light."

Kate Phillips, the BBC's chief content officer, said it was hoped the 30-minute documentary "will resonate with BBC viewers and provide comfort and support to those navigating their own health challenges".

Catherine was treated at The Royal Marsden Hospital and funds from the distribution of this documentary, which is to be broadcast in other countries, will be paid to The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity.

When cancer patients finish treatment at the London hospital they can symbolically ring a bell.

"I didn't ring the bell," says Catherine, speaking to her brother James Middleton.

"Maybe this is your ringing the bell," he says, about carrying out the Three Peaks Challenge and this documentary about her healing.

Heal will be shown on BBC iPlayer from 12:00 GMT and BBC One at 18:40 GMT on 29 November. It will also air internationally, including on NBCUniversal in the US on 30 November, Channel 9 in Australia on 1 December and CTV and Noovo in Canada on 7 December

articles.title: Devon sessions offer advice on rising energy costs
articles.summary: A council is urging people to seek support with rising energy costs on heating this winter.
articles.body:
A charity is offering free advice on energy bills with prices expected to climb further from January .

Devon Communities Together said it was hosting drop-in sessions across the county, which include help with energy bills, smart meters and switching suppliers.

Gas and electricity bills for a typical household are forecast to rise by £443 a year from January. Heating oil prices have also risen drastically since the start of this year , from about 60p to £1.11 a litre, according to the Action with Communities in Rural England network.

Devon County Council said many households in rural parts relied on heating oil because they were not connected to mains gas.

Nora Corkery, chief executive of Devon Communities Together, said: "Behind every statistic is a household making difficult choices: rationing the heating, putting off filling up a tank, or cutting back on journeys they can't really do without."

The charity said people could access confidential one-to-one support to find financial help, with a limited number of free winter warm packs available for those who attend.

Cheryl Cottle-Hunkin, from Devon County Council, said: "I'd urge anyone who is struggling, or worried about the winter ahead, to seek advice and find out what help may be available."

More information on the sessions was available on the charity's website .

articles.title: Endangered red squirrels thriving on British island
articles.summary: Conservationists say that, with red squirrels dwindling in the UK, Jersey is an "important refuge".
articles.body:
With growing concerns that red squirrels could soon become extinct in England , one Channel Island is a corner of the British Isles where they maintain a stronghold.

Jersey is home to a thriving red squirrel population, thanks to the complete absence of grey squirrels, which carry a virus deadly to their red cousins.

Red squirrels are endangered in the UK , with about 120,000 to 160,000 left in the wild and various projects are aiming to boost those numbers.

There have some strongholds in England , particularly islands, and 75% of the British population is in Scotland .

However, despite not being native to Jersey, Henry Glynn, an ecologist with the National Trust of Jersey, said they "really are iconic for Jersey".

He said: "When you speak to people who have come over to visit the island from the UK, a lot of them will say that one of the things they want to do whilst here is to see a red squirrel, because they're so rare and so difficult to see in large parts of the UK.

"That is actually really special for them."

Red squirrels are not native to Jersey, having been introduced in 1885.

However, Glynn described them as "naturalised", having become "assimilated into the natural environment" over many years.

The animals have previously featured in Visit Jersey tourism campaigns, including one fronted by conservationist Ben Fogle.

The National Trust of Jersey said the island wa s an "important refuge" for the red squirrel, where they were " fairly widespread ".

It said the inland valleys and woodlands were the best places to spot them.

The species is legally protected, which means it would be a criminal offence to harm them.

Nina Powell, senior animal carer at the JSPCA [Jersey Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals], said Jersey has a "good population" of squirrels and that "you can see them almost anywhere".

While the primary reason for their success is the lack of grey squirrels, Powell said they also thrived "because people look out for them".

She said: "A lot of people do support them, put out feeders and stuff like that.

"Their habitats are decreasing everywhere... but we do have quite a lot of nature reserves.

"In some places, we've got rope bridges which really help them cross the roads, and our speed limits are quite low, so that helps them as well".

She said the JSPCA had handled 50 red squirrels so far this year, including hand-raising eight babies, called kits (kittens).

She said: "We want to keep all animals as wild as possible, so we try and be as hands-off as possible.

"Some of them don't like us... some of them are quite sweet. They really do vary in personality."

Glynn agreed that their success had come in part because of the efforts of islanders.

He said: "They're really beloved amongst the local community as well. A lot of people put out squirrel feeders or love to see them in the garden.

"We get lots of reports from people who just want to tell us they've seen them because they're so happy to have them around."

articles.title: Sudan’s elderly face hardship and heartbreak in a life of displacement
articles.summary: Sudan’s displaced elderly often have to support grandchildren or fend for themselves.
articles.body:
Khartoum, Sudan – Hamad Mohammed Adam, 70, should be spending his days surrounded by his family and enjoying the comfort of life in his home village. Instead, he finds himself among hundreds of displaced elderly people in a camp in western Omdurman, with little between him and death.

Three months ago, Adam’s life changed when the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary attacked his village near Bara, northern Kordofan. He followed the rest of the village and fled, leaving behind his home, belongings and most painfully, his family.

“It was an early morning last August when the Rapid Support Forces militia invaded our village near Bara. It was a terrifying morning; they were killing everyone, women, men, children,” he said. “I ran with some friends and spent days to reach Omdurman. I am lucky that I have survived, but I am worried about my family.”

The war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the RSF paramilitary, two former military allies now engaged in a bitter power struggle for Sudan since April 2023, has affected all parts of the country. When fighting erupts in one area, residents are often forced to flee to another, where they lack jobs, a home, or a support base.

After travelling for about 300km (186 miles), Adam found himself in western Omdurman, close to the capital Khartoum. Today, he resides at al-Moulih camp for displaced people in western Omdurman, home to approximately 10,000 people, with those aged over 65 accounting for about one in five residents.

His escape from the fighting between the SAF and RSF, which has triggered one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, was only the start of his troubles. Adam knows nothing about the whereabouts of his family, and they don’t know where he is.

Lacking the support of his family, Adam’s immediate concern is finding enough food, medication and healthcare to survive. But the uncertainty of his family’s fate weighs heavily on him every day.

In the same camp, Aisha Alneel, 70, has lost more than her home: The security, independence and family connections that once shaped her life. She’s accompanied by her 72-year-old sister who needs medical attention, and her greatest hope is to reunite with her family and regain some sense of normality.

“I came to Port Sudan two years ago after losing my home in Khartoum. My plan is to travel with my older sister, but we faced financial strain,” she said. “We preferred to stay at this displacement camp in Port Sudan until we have enough money to leave.”

Sudan’s older population, classified as aged above 65 by the United Nations, is 1.8 million people in 2026, accounting for 3.5% of the population, according to the UN’s Economic and Social Commission for Western Asia.

Many elderly displaced people depend on regular medical supervision and assistance with everyday activities. When conflict forces them to abandon their homes, families, and familiar environments, these essential support systems can disappear overnight. It also disrupts or destroys the infrastructure and services they relied on to maintain a dignified life.

Traditionally, Sudanese families and local communities played a central role in caring for older relatives. Younger family members often assisted with food, medical appointments and daily needs, but the war has seen families scattered across Sudan and the country’s social fabric destroyed.

Living standards have plunged to levels last seen in the early 1990s, making it difficult for families to survive, let alone provide support to others. The UNDP has noted that Sudan’s economy has shrunk by more than 40 percent since the war broke out, and extreme poverty is expected to rise above 60 percent. This has placed additional pressure on institutions responsible for caring for older people.

At Al-Daw Hajooj home for the elderly, the management faces the difficult task of providing care to senior citizens amid a wider humanitarian crisis.

Moubarak Satti, director of Al-Daw Hajooj, told Al Jazeera that the home has 11 seniors and the situation remains “difficult” due to a lack of financial support needed to run the elderly care programmes.

“Like many institutions, we have been severely affected by the war. We lost our only vehicle, which we use it to transport elderly people to medical facilities; we lost many people during the conflict due to the lack of medical care,” Satti said.

“We welcome financial support from the community, NGOs, and international humanitarian organisations to continue providing care and essential services to older people.”

This requires more than emergency food assistance. It needs a coordinated response that recognises elderly people as a particular group with specific needs, said Satti.

The strain of displacement also impacts older people’s mental and emotional wellbeing. Separation from children and grandchildren, uncertainty about the future, and feelings of anxiety and helplessness can create intense feelings of isolation, government officials have said.

The Khartoum State Ministry of Social Development has provided support to vulnerable groups, such as the elderly, coordinating social protection services and working with relevant institutions to respond to the needs of displaced communities.

But the scale of the problem is staggering, with about 8.6 million people currently displaced. Attacks on civilian areas have also severely disrupted public services, making government and NGO support increasingly challenging, Minister of Social Welfare Siddig Ferini told Al Jazeera.

“We have reunited dozens of elderly displaced people with their families in many Sudanese states, while others are still searching for loved ones,” Ferini said. “We call on humanitarian organisations, donors, and philanthropists to support elderly people through social care and essential services, especially amid the ongoing war and economic crisis.”
